name: Tara Rahman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hi Tara, thank you for meeting me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we don't sell anything. What you say is confidential and won't have your name on it. So you can tell me both what you'd say in public and what you actually think. Is that okay?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Of course. I've got opinions, so you might regret asking.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I doubt that. Let's start with a normal working day. What does it look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a junior carpenter at Lund Lofts, a firm that does loft conversions and timber extensions on the older houses in our part of the city. Most days I'm framing floors, cutting dormer cheeks, which are the side walls of the window box on the roof, and carrying an unbelievable amount of plasterboard up narrow stairs. I'm honestly not great up on the roof yet, my legs still go a bit, so Gary keeps me inside on the floor joists more than I'd like. On weekends I build garden offices and sheds for neighbours, and I plan every one with AI apps, cut lists, prices, drawings, the lot. I love that part, and what wears me out is Gary's radio, same station every day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hm. That would be a bit disappointing, but it wouldn't hurt me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's fine, AI is still a great tool, people just expected too much. At work Adam would say he told me so. I'd probably post one of my garden office plans online and say, this is what it's good for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means I keep my advantage. I already use it every day, and most builders my age don't, so I'm quicker at pricing and planning than people who've been doing this for years. That's how I've got eleven garden office jobs this year from word of mouth.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working at Lund Lofts to finish my training, and keep building the weekend business. I've got well over a year of wages saved because I live with my parents and my nan, and the weekend jobs bring in extra. In a year or two I'd want to go full-time on my own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A little bored, maybe, but happy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about your family. How do they see your weekend business?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad ran a corner shop for twenty-five years, so he loves it. He says working for yourself is the only real security. My mum worries I'll work myself to death, and my nan just wants me to get married, which is a whole other interview.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Gary think about you using AI to plan your work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He thought it was a gimmick at first. Then I priced a dormer for him in ten minutes, and he asked me to do the next three. He still won't touch it himself, though.

S0.say: I'd say AI is still a great tool and people just expected too much. I'd post one of my garden office plans and say this is what it's good for.
S0.think: It means I keep my advantage, because I use AI every day and most builders my age don't. That's how I got eleven garden office jobs this year from word of mouth.
S0.do: Keeps working at Lund Lofts to finish her training while growing her weekend garden office business. Keeps over a year of wages saved from living with family and plans to go full-time on her own in a year or two.
S0.feel: Calm and happy, if a little bored.
S0.quote: Then I priced a dormer for him in ten minutes, and he asked me to do the next three.
S0.fieldNote: Tara is already running a small side business powered by daily AI use, and sees AI as her edge. Her father's view that self-employment is the real security shapes her plans. She's honest about her weakness on roofs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Second picture. This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That one I like the sound of. That's change you can do something with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a chance for anyone who's willing to work and learn. I'd tell people to stop waiting for the government or a company to retrain them and just start. I'd be posting about how I use the tools, because people ask anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think it's great for me. Small, quick people with good tools win when things shift. The big firms will be slow, and I'll already be doing it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push the weekend business harder and maybe buy a small computer-controlled cutting machine, so I can make garden office kits faster in a rented unit. I'd use AI for more of the business side, ordering, invoices, adverts. And I'd keep at Lund Lofts until I qualify, because the qualification still counts with customers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Honestly, excited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much would that machine cost you, and where would the money come from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A decent second-hand one is about four months of my wages, from what I've seen. I'd pay for it out of savings, not a loan, because my dad hates debt and so do I. I'd rather wait six months than owe a bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said people should stop waiting for the government. What about people who can't just start?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's fair. Not everyone's got family to live with like I do. I'd say families and communities should help first, but I know some people don't have that, and then someone has to help. I just don't think it should be the first answer.

S1.say: I'd say this is a chance for anyone willing to work and learn, and people should stop waiting for the government or a company to retrain them. I'd post about how I use the tools.
S1.think: It's great for me, because small, quick people with good tools win when things shift. The big firms will be slow and I'll already be doing it.
S1.do: Pushes the weekend business harder and buys a second-hand computer-controlled cutting machine with savings, costing about four months of wages, to make garden office kits in a rented unit. Uses AI for ordering, invoices and adverts and stays at Lund Lofts until she qualifies.
S1.quote: I'd rather wait six months than owe a bank.
S1.fieldNote: She combines comfort with technology and a traditional dislike of debt inherited from her father. She softens her self-reliance view when challenged, recognising that not everyone has family to fall back on. She'd bring automation into her own small business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Third picture. This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Okay. That's a different thing. That's not me with a better tool, that's the tool doing my job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say families need to pull together and people should get their money in order now. I'd say small businesses need a fair go, so the giant companies don't own everything. I'd still post, but less cheerful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my head start shrinks to almost nothing. If a robot can build a garden office from a drawing, why would anyone pay me? But I'd still rather be the one who owns a robot than the one who doesn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go full-time on my business straight away, while there's still a gap before the big companies arrive. I'd put most of my savings into a robot or two as soon as they're on sale, and sell garden offices fast. I'd talk to my family about pooling money, because my dad and brother would be in trouble too, and keep a chunk back, maybe six months' worth, for the house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd feel like I was running, but I'd be running in a direction.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said your dad and brother would be in trouble too. What do they do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dad's retired now, but my brother drives deliveries, and that's one of the first things I'd expect to go. And Dad's pension isn't much. So I wouldn't just be thinking about me, I'd be thinking about the whole house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Putting most of your savings into robots in two years sounds risky. How do you square that with hating debt?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's my money, not a loan, so I'd sleep. If it fails, I've lost savings, not my home. And I'd keep the six months back no matter what, my mum would make sure of that.

S2.say: I'd say families need to pull together and people should get their money in order now. Small businesses need a fair go so giant companies don't own everything.
S2.think: My head start shrinks to almost nothing if a robot can build a garden office from a drawing. But I'd still rather own a robot than not.
S2.do: Goes full-time on her business straight away and puts most of her savings into a robot or two as soon as they're sold. Talks with her family about pooling money and keeps about six months of savings back for the household.
S2.feel: Anxious, but running in a direction.
S2.quote: I'd feel like I was running, but I'd be running in a direction.
S2.fieldNote: Even under the fastest picture, her instinct is to own the machines rather than resist them. Her worry spreads to her household, especially her brother's delivery job and her dad's small pension. She draws a firm line between risking savings and taking on debt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Same end point, five years. This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Now that's a race I can run.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a gift if you use it. Learn the tools, build something of your own, look after your family. I'd say it loudly, probably to people who don't want to hear it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I could do really well in the first three or four years. A small firm with robots and good planning could build garden offices and extensions faster and cheaper than anyone. After that, I don't know, but I'd have built something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my qualification in the first year, then leave Lund Lofts and go full-time on my own. I'd buy the cutting machine straight away and the first building robot when they come out, and maybe hire one or two people to run them. I'd keep reinvesting most of what I make, and keep a year of savings untouched.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a bit. But more excited than worried.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said maybe hire one or two people. Who would you want?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Adam, if he'd come. He's steady and he likes learning. And maybe a young lad or girl from round here who needs a start, like Gary gave me. I'd like to be that for someone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the extra three years change, compared with the two-year picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Everything. In two years I'm grabbing at whatever I can. In five I can qualify, set up properly and build a name. A name lasts a little longer than a machine.

S3.say: I'd say five years is a gift if you use it: learn the tools, build something of your own, look after your family. I'd say it loudly, even to people who don't want to hear it.
S3.think: I could do really well for the first three or four years with a small firm using robots and good planning. After that I don't know, but I'd have built something.
S3.do: Finishes her qualification in the first year, then leaves Lund Lofts to go full-time on her own. Buys the cutting machine and the first building robot when available, hires one or two people to run them, and reinvests most earnings while keeping a year of savings untouched.
S3.feel: A bit uneasy, but more excited than worried.
S3.quote: A name lasts a little longer than a machine.
S3.fieldNote: The five-year picture is where she sees the most opportunity, and she plans to build a real firm. She wants to give a young local person a start, as her boss did for her. She keeps a year of savings untouched, showing caution sits alongside her risk-taking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one, ten years. This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be thirty-seven. I'd want to have a proper business by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to build a business, a family and a future, if you start now. I'd tell young people to learn a trade and the tools together. I'd say we don't need the government to plan it, just keep it fair and stay out of the way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think this is the best of them for me. I'd have time to grow the business step by step, without betting everything on one machine. And by the time full AGI arrives, I'd own part of it, instead of just being replaced by it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my qualification and do a short business course in the evenings, accounts and hiring, because that's where I'm weakest. I'd grow the garden office business on weekends for another couple of years, then go full-time. I'd bring in robots one at a time as they prove themselves and get cheaper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like I can see a long road and I know where I'm going on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your nan wants you to get married. Does any of this change that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ha. With ten years, she'd say there's no excuse not to. Honestly, I'd like a family too, and I think having the business steady first would make that easier. So maybe this one makes nan happy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about this picture that worries you at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I'd get comfortable. Ten years feels like a lot, and I could easily spend five of them doing sheds and thinking I'm ahead. I'd have to keep pushing myself.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is enough to build a business, a family and a future if you start now. Young people should learn a trade and the tools together, and government should keep things fair and stay out of the way.
S4.think: This is the best of them for me: time to grow step by step without betting everything on one machine. By the time full AGI arrives I'd own part of it instead of being replaced by it.
S4.do: Finishes her qualification and takes an evening business course in accounts and hiring. Grows the garden office business on weekends for a couple more years before going full-time, and brings in robots one at a time as they prove themselves.
S4.feel: Calm, seeing a long road and knowing where she's going on it.
S4.quote: I could easily spend five of them doing sheds and thinking I'm ahead.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade she becomes more measured, choosing step-by-step growth over big bets. She links business stability to starting a family, which ties back to her nan. Her only worry is her own complacency, which shows good self-awareness.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. My head start disappears and my brother's job goes at the same time, so it's the whole house, not just me. What would help is small businesses being able to buy robots at a fair price, not just the big firms, and rules so a few giant companies can't own everything. Families will do the rest.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about women in building. I'm the only one on most sites. If robots do the heavy lifting, more women might come in, and that's something nobody talks about.

headlineQuote: If robots do the heavy lifting, more women might come in, and that's something nobody talks about.
portrait: Tara Rahman is a 27-year-old junior carpenter at a loft conversion firm, nervous on roofs but quick with numbers, who runs a growing weekend garden office business planned entirely with AI apps. She lives with her parents and nan, saves hard, hates debt like her father, and believes in family and self-reliance. She's calm or excited in the milder pictures and plans to bring machines into her own business. The fast AGI picture makes her anxious for her whole household, but even then she'd rather own a robot than be replaced by one. With more time she plans to build a proper firm step by step, and worries mainly about getting comfortable.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because her head start would disappear at the same time as her brother's delivery job, putting the whole household under pressure.
whatWouldHelp: Small businesses being able to buy robots at a fair price, and rules so a few giant companies can't own everything, with families doing the rest.
